eyebrow: Python for Data Science · Chapter 3, Lesson 12
subtitle: The two-minute routine to run before you trust any dataset.

code:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

# order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount, status
# order 5 has an empty amount on purpose
caption: Real data is never perfectly complete — this orders table has one missing amount.

code:
orders.head(3)
#   order_id customer_id order_date  amount   status
# 0        1         101 2024-01-05  120.50  shipped
# 1        2         102 2024-01-07   89.99  shipped

# orders.tail(3) checks the other end
caption: head(n)/tail(n) default to 5 rows — checking both ends catches a wrong header or a stray total row.

code:
orders.info()
# RangeIndex: 8 entries, 0 to 7
#  order_id     8 non-null   int64
#  amount       7 non-null   float64
#  order_date   8 non-null   object   <- text, not a date!
caption: amount shows only 7 non-null (one's missing); order_date read as object is the most common surprise.

code:
orders.describe()
# amount: count 7, min 45.0, max 310.0, mean, std, quartiles

orders.describe(include="object")
# count, unique, top value, frequency
caption: describe() happily averages an ID column too — pandas can't know which numbers are really labels.
isna() flags True/False per cell; sum() adds up the Trues per column.

code:
o2 = pd.read_csv("orders.csv",
                  parse_dates=["order_date"],
                  usecols=["order_id", "order_date", "amount"])
o2.dtypes
# order_date    datetime64[ns]
caption: parse_dates converts to real dates; usecols keeps only what you need; nrows previews a huge file.

subtitle: Choosing exactly the rows and columns you want.
